headline: Halfway Rock Holds Its Groundfish While Bass Work the Island Edges
subhead: Cooler bay water is keeping the bite honest through midday, even as the mackerel run thins and cod settle deeper on the ledges.
body_markdown:
I was out past Peaks Island Tuesday morning, drifting the eastern edge where the current pulls hard around the ledge on the last of the ebb, and I noticed something I make a point of noticing every August: the gulls weren't working the surface the way they were in June. That's not a bad sign — it's a seasonal one. The mackerel schools that the bay in May and June have scattered and thinned, the way they always do once the water settles into its summer rhythm. What's left are smaller, tighter pods, and you have to hunt for them now rather than simply follow the birds.

I found one such pod off the Portland breakwater in about 40 feet, marked heavy on the sounder, and put two mackerel trees down on light spinning gear for maybe twenty minutes of steady action before they moved off. That's the pattern this week — good but not sustained, here and gone in a tide cycle. If you're after fresh bait for bass or bluefish, I'd treat any mackerel showing as a window, not a guarantee, and fish it hard the moment you find it.

The striped bass have been the more dependable story, and the reason is straightforward: Casco Bay's water hasn't overheated the way it has south of Cape Cod. Down there, stripers have gone nocturnal, pushed deep by water sitting in the mid-70s. Up here, the Gulf of Maine keeps feeding us cooler water through the tidal exchange, and the bass are still willing to work the flats and ledges well into the afternoon. I had good luck working the Bailey Island shoreline on the last two hours of the incoming, casting a 1-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse tail tight along the rockweed edge, letting it sink before a slow, methodical retrieve — the same approach that produces results on any current seam where bait gets pinned against structure. Fish in the mid-20-inch range, a few pushing 30, mixed with shorts that kept things interesting for anyone fishing with kids or students, which I still do more often than I probably should admit.

Harpswell's back channels and the mouth of the Basin have been holding fish too, particularly on the moving tide when bait gets funneled through the narrows. Live mackerel under a slip float, or a swimming plug worked slow through the current seam, has been the more consistent producer there than anything worked fast. Two Lights, characteristically, has been a dawn spot — surface activity for maybe forty minutes around first light before the fish drop back down, so if you're fishing that stretch, get there before the sun clears the horizon or don't bother.

Bluefish have started showing in numbers I'd call notable for early August — not blitzing yet, but present in the coves around Peaks and in the channel off Portland, chasing whatever bait concentrates near the surface. We flagged this pattern building a few weeks back, and it's holding — wherever the bait schools tighten up, the blues are finding them and feeding hard for short stretches. Snapper-sized fish are thick in the shallower coves for anyone wanting light-tackle action, and the adult fish have been mixed in with the mackerel schools, so don't be surprised if your mackerel jig comes back missing its tail.

Halfway Rock remains the most reliable groundfish structure in the bay, and this week reinforced why I keep sending people there rather than the closer, shallower ledges. Cod and haddock have settled into 70 to 90 feet on the northeast side, and the bite has been a slack-tide affair — you want that window when the current eases enough to hold bottom without a pound of lead, jigging diamond jigs or drifting clam baits along the structure. It's not a fast bite this time of year; midsummer groundfish fishing rarely is. But it's been steady enough that two or three fish per trip in the 3-to-6-pound range isn't unusual for anyone willing to work the ledge methodically rather than drift through it once and move on.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to shift dramatically. The bay's thermal structure has been stable, and as long as that stable weather window holds, I'd expect the same daytime striper activity along the island edges and the same slack-tide groundfish bite at Halfway Rock. If the wind stays out of the southwest and the tides keep building the way they have, I'd put my time on the incoming at Bailey Island for bass and slack water at Halfway Rock for bottom fish. Watch for the mackerel schools to keep contracting through August — by month's end, you may be relying more on jigs and metal than trees to raise them at all.
